name: Tomas Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. What you say is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a sales negotiator at the Elm Parade branch of Brightwell Homes, a regional chain with about thirty offices. Most of what I sell is two and three-bed family houses in a commuter town, people moving out of the city for a garden. A day is chasing buyers' mortgage offers, two or three viewings, a valuation if the manager lets me, and a lot of phone calls to solicitors asking why nothing's moved.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is when a chain of four sales finally all exchange on the same afternoon and everyone's happy at once. Worst is the waiting, weeks of solicitors and surveys where I can't do anything. My pay is a basic plus commission, so a slow month really shows.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at work now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. A colleague, Dev, showed me how to get a draft of a listing description from one of the chat tools, and I use it when I've got six to write. I always rewrite it, because it says every kitchen is stunning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that got oversold, which is what I've thought all along. It writes a first draft of a listing, it sorts my emails a bit, and that's about it. At the Friday drinks I'd probably joke that Dev owes us all an apology for the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job stays basically what it is, and that's fine by me. The real risk to my pay is the market, interest rates and whether people keep moving. Priya, my partner, is a primary teacher, so we've got one steady salary between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the listing drafts to save an hour a week. I'd keep saving toward a deposit for our own place, we're at about four months of bills put aside. Maybe I'd finally sit the valuation course Brightwell keeps offering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, honestly. It's the world I already know how to work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a slow month shows in your pay. How slow does it have to get before you worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If commission halved for three months in a row, I'd worry. That happened once, in a winter when rates jumped, and we ate a lot of pasta. Priya's salary covers the rent, so it's never been a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra hour a week change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it on the phone with buyers, which is where sales actually happen. An hour more of real talking with buyers a week is worth more to me than any fancy report. Brightwell's head office would probably just give us a bigger target, mind.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **decent tool** that got oversold.
I'd joke that the **hype merchants** owe everyone an apology.
think: My job stays **the same**, and the real risk is the **housing market**.
Priya's teacher salary gives us **one steady income** under the commission swings.
do: Keep using **listing drafts** to save about an hour a week.
Keep saving toward a **house deposit** from a four-month cushion.
Sit the **valuation course** Brightwell keeps offering.
feel: **Relaxed**, because it's the world he already knows how to work in.
S0.quote: An hour more of real talking with buyers a week is worth more to me than any fancy report.
fieldNote: His calm rests on **Priya's salary**; commission alone would make him less sure.
He frames AI as a **time-saver** that pushes him back to phone work.
There's a quiet note of **suspicion** that head office would turn saved time into targets.

steps.text: Use chat-tool listing drafts to save an hour weekly
Keep adding to the house deposit fund each month
Sit the Brightwell valuation course before the spring market

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that firms need to share the gains with staff, not just shrink the office. If software books viewings, writes listings and answers enquiries, Brightwell will run branches with half the people. I'd say that to the area manager and I'd say it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job splits in two. The paperwork half, chasing, writing, booking, goes to software. The half that's left is the viewings, the valuations and talking a nervous seller off the ledge, and they'll want fewer of us doing more of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools properly once a couple of branches had shown they work, not before. I'd push hard to get onto valuations, because that's the face-to-face bit that lasts. And I'd talk to the others about whether a staff association could get us something in writing on job cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. I'm average at this job, and average is the first thing that gets trimmed when a branch shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the branch would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karen on the front desk, who answers the phone and books everything. That's exactly the work the card lists. And probably the newest negotiator, because last in is first out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for proof before learning the tools. What counts as proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two or three branches using it for six months without sales falling apart. I've seen head office roll out things that got quietly dropped. But once Dev's branch is selling more with it, I'm on it the next week.

say: I'd say firms must **share the gains** instead of shrinking the office.
I'd tell the area manager that **half-staffed branches** will hurt sellers and buyers.
think: My job **splits in two**: paperwork goes to software, viewings and valuations stay.
Being **average** at the job makes me easy to trim when branches shrink.
do: Learn the **new tools** properly once a few branches prove them.
Push to get onto **valuations**, the face-to-face work that lasts.
Start talking with colleagues about a **staff association**.
feel: **Uneasy** turning into worried about being trimmed for being average.
S1.quote: I'm average at this job, and average is the first thing that gets trimmed when a branch shrinks.
fieldNote: He clearly sees which **half of his job** goes first, and plans around the half that stays.
His **steady** style shows: he'll adopt once he sees proof, not before.
Concern for **Karen** on the front desk mixes with self-interest.

steps.text: Learn Brightwell's booking software once three branches use it well
Ask the branch manager to train me on valuations
Sound out colleagues about forming a staff association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an emergency and the government should treat it like one, with income support straight away. You can't let millions of office jobs go in two years and just hope. I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job shrinks to nothing in two years, apart from showing people round. And with the robots three years behind, maybe a few of us survive as tour guides until 2031. That's not a career, that's a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the house deposit plan and keep the cash where we can reach it. I'd look at jobs where a person is the point, like housing support work or teaching assistant work alongside Priya's school. I'd also join a union, any union that would have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Two years is less time than my partner Priya and I have been saving for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're not buying the house, not yet. Priya would probably be relieved and annoyed at once, because she was the one who wanted the garden. Then we'd make a list of what her job and mine look like in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is any of your work safe for those first three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Viewings, a bit. People still want to stand in a kitchen with someone and ask about the neighbours. But one person can do that for the whole town if everything else is done by software, so it's not three years of safety for all of us.

say: I'd call it an **emergency** needing income support straight away.
I'd sign every **petition** for the people losing office jobs.
think: My job shrinks to **showing people round**, and that only until the robots arrive.
Viewings won't keep a **whole branch** employed, just one person per town.
do: Pause the **house deposit** plan and keep savings in easy reach.
Apply for **housing support** or teaching assistant work.
Join a **union** within the first months.
feel: **Scared**, because two years is shorter than their house saving plan.
S2.quote: Two years is less time than my partner Priya and I have been saving for a house.
fieldNote: He expects to lose **most of his income** and treats the robot gap as no comfort.
The **house purchase** is the first casualty, which he'd tell his partner the same night.
He looks for work where **a person** is the point, a clear thread in his thinking.

steps.text: Pause the house purchase and keep savings in an instant-access account
Apply for housing support worker jobs in the first months
Join a union and sign petitions for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's enough to be sensible if we start now. Retraining money, notice periods, and a tax on firms that cut people for software. I'd say that at work too, even to the area manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I've got about three good years left in sales. Then the thinking side goes, and the viewings follow when the robots come in 2034. I'd be thirty-two and I'd want to be somewhere else by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools fully once they're common, to sell more while selling still pays. I'd bank the extra commission and get the cushion to six months. Around year two I'd start a part-time course in social housing management and move across by year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but organised. It's less a shock and more a plan with a date on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use the tools to sell more, even while they're replacing people. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'd still be arguing for rules at the same time. Refusing the AI tools wouldn't save anyone's job at Brightwell, it would just cost me commission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but smaller, and only once I've got the housing job lined up. A mortgage on commission pay in that world would be mad. Priya and I would rent a couple more years.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to be sensible if we start now.
I'd push for a **tax on firms** that swap people for software.
think: I've got about **three good years** left in sales.
By **thirty-two** I want to be in different work.
do: Use AI tools to **sell more** while selling still pays.
Bank extra commission to reach a **six-month cushion**.
Train in **social housing management** and switch by year four.
feel: **Worried but organised**, with a date to plan around.
S3.quote: Refusing the AI tools wouldn't save anyone's job at Brightwell, it would just cost me commission.
fieldNote: He admits the **contradiction** between using the tools and wanting rules, and accepts it.
Five years turns his alarm into a **staged plan** with dates.
The house is **delayed, not dropped**, which shows some hope.

steps.text: Use AI booking and listing tools daily to raise sales
Bank extra commission until savings cover six months
Start a part-time social housing management course in year two
Rent two more years before buying a smaller house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's not waste it arguing about whether it's real. Get proper retraining set up, protect people's pay while they switch. I'd say it calmly, which is new for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough for me to do one more proper stretch in sales and then move. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, with a skill that still works with people. That feels doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep selling and get onto valuations properly over the next two years. We'd buy the house in year two or three, a smaller one we could pay with Priya's salary alone. Then I'd retrain into housing or something similar around year five, while I still have a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It feels like a long runway rather than a cliff edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a house you could pay on one salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if my work goes, we can't be stuck. Priya's job looks safer for longer, kids still need a teacher in the room. Our house has to fit my partner Priya's teacher salary, because my estate agent pay might not last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do at Brightwell differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to test the new systems, once they're properly working. If I'm going to leave in five years, I want to leave knowing how this stuff works, not as the bloke who refused it.

say: I'd say we have **a decade**, so stop arguing about whether it's real.
I'd ask for **retraining with pay protection** for people who switch.
think: Ten years gives me **one more stretch** in sales before moving on.
At thirty-seven I'd still have a **people skill** worth something.
do: Get onto **valuations** properly within two years.
Buy a **smaller house** that Priya's salary alone could pay.
Retrain into **housing work** around year five.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, like having a long runway.
S4.quote: Our house has to fit my partner Priya's teacher salary, because my estate agent pay might not last.
fieldNote: With ten years, he still expects to leave sales, but on **his own timing**.
The **one-salary house** rule shows careful planning around the household.
He'd volunteer to **test new systems**, a shift from wait-and-see.

steps.text: Train as a valuer at Brightwell over two years
Buy a small house Priya's salary alone could cover
Volunteer to test Brightwell's new AI systems

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It lands before we've bought a house and before I've got another skill. What would help is income support for people in office jobs, and free courses into work like housing or care.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about buyers. People buying their first house are scared and they want a person telling them it's going to be fine. I don't know if a machine can do that, even a very clever one.

headlineQuote: People buying their first house are scared and they want a person telling them it's going to be fine.
portrait: Tomas is a **sales negotiator** at a regional chain, selling family homes in a commuter town.
He lives with Priya, a **primary teacher**, and they're saving for a house deposit.
He uses AI **now and then**, rewriting every draft, and waits for proof before adopting more.
Faster scenarios make him **pause the house**, join a union and look at housing support work.
With more time he plans **valuations, then housing work**, and buys a home on one salary.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands before they buy a house or he has another skill.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** for office workers and **free courses** into housing or care.
